{{format footnotes |date=May 2024}}
In mathematics, the '''Peters polynomials''' ''s''<sub>''n''</sub>(''x'') are polynomials studied by George Peters<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Schafer |first=R. D. |date=1956-01-01 |title=The October meeting in College Park |url=http://www.ams.org/journal-getitem?pii=S0002-9904-1956-09972-0 |journal=Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society |language=en |volume=62 |issue=1 |pages=1–13 |doi=10.1090/S0002-9904-1956-09972-0 |issn=0002-9904|doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Schafer |first=R. D. |date=1956-07-01 |title=The April meeting in New York |url=http://www.ams.org/journal-getitem?pii=S0002-9904-1956-10046-3 |journal=Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society |language=en |volume=62 |issue=4 |pages=369–401 |doi=10.1090/S0002-9904-1956-10046-3 |issn=0002-9904|doi-access=free }}</ref> given by the [[generating function]]

:<math>\displaystyle \sum_{n=0}^{+\infty} s_n(x)\frac{t^n}{n!} = \frac{(1+t)^x}{(1+(1+t)^\lambda)^{\mu}}</math>

{{harv|Roman|1984|loc=4.4.6}}, {{harv|Boas|Buck|1958|loc=p.37}}. They are a generalization of the [[Boole polynomials]].
